read.sections.0.heading.source: One object can have many meanings
read.sections.0.heading.back: One object can have many meanings

read.sections.0.text.note: "skill" (a weaver's craft) = ฝีมือ throughout this lesson rather than ทักษะ (KEY_TERMS' word for "skill" on teachers' pages); ฝีมือ reads more naturally for handwork. The educator note keeps ทักษะ for "the main skill" learners practise.
read.sections.0.text.source: Look at the woven bag in the evidence. The seller says it is made for carrying food and books. That is its practical use. The owner says an aunt gave it to them when they started at a new school, so the bag also holds a memory. The makers, a craft group, learned the pattern from older weavers. For them, the bag shows a skill. It is one bag, but each person sees it from a different perspective. To understand an object, you need its context: who made it, who uses it, and why.
read.sections.0.text.back: Look at the woven bag in the evidence. The seller says the bag was made for carrying food and books. That is its use. The owner says an aunt gave the bag when they started at a new school, so the bag holds a memory too. The bag's makers are a craft group who learned this pattern from older weavers. For them, the bag shows skill. There is one bag, but each person sees it from a different perspective. To understand an object, you need to know its context: who made it, who uses it and why.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Look at the woven bag. The seller says it carries food and books. That is its use. The owner got it as a gift when they started at a new school. Context means who made it, who uses it, and why.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Objects carry meaning around the world
read.sections.1.heading.back: Objects have meaning all over the world

read.sections.1.text.note: kente = ผ้าเคนเต, batik = ผ้าบาติก, tapa = ผ้าทาปา, Tonga = ตองกา, Fiji = ฟิจิ, Ghana = กานา. "proverbs" = สุภาษิต (standard), "wise words" in the simpler text = คำสอน.
read.sections.1.text.source: Many communities make objects with cultural meaning. In Ghana, weavers make kente cloth from narrow strips that are sewn together. Many kente patterns have names, and some names come from proverbs or events in history. In Indonesia, people decorate batik cloth with hot wax and dye. Batik is used through life, from cloths that carry babies to clothes for weddings. In the Pacific, in places such as Tonga and Fiji, people beat tree bark to make tapa cloth. Groups often make it together, and it is used at weddings and other big events.
read.sections.1.text.back: Many communities make objects with cultural meaning. In Ghana, weavers make kente cloth from narrow strips sewn together. Many kente patterns have names, and some names come from proverbs or events in history. In Indonesia, people decorate batik cloth with hot wax and dye. Batik is used throughout life, from cloth for carrying babies to clothes at weddings. In the Pacific, in places such as Tonga and Fiji, people beat tree bark to make tapa cloth. People often gather in groups to make it, and use the cloth at weddings and other important events.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Many groups make things with cultural meaning. In Ghana, people weave kente cloth. Many kente patterns have names. Some names come from wise words or past events. In Indonesia, people make batik with wax and dye. They use it for babies and at weddings. In the Pacific, people make tapa cloth from tree bark. Groups often make it together. They use it at big events.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Many groups make things with cultural meaning. In Ghana people weave kente cloth. Many kente patterns have names. Some names come from teachings or past events. In Indonesia people make batik cloth with wax and dye. They use this cloth with babies and at weddings. In the Pacific, people make tapa cloth from tree bark. People often make it together in groups. They use this cloth at important events.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Ask before you explain an object
read.sections.2.heading.back: Ask before you explain an object

read.sections.2.text.note: "It is also a mistake to guess" = ก็ไม่ถูกต้องเช่นกัน (avoids ผิด); "is weak" = เป็นป้ายที่ไม่หนักแน่น, and "stronger" in the quick check = หนักแน่นขึ้น.
read.sections.2.text.source: A museum label tells visitors about an object. The first label for the bag says only “Everyday carrying bag”. That is true, but it misses the memory and the skill. It is also a mistake to guess what the pattern means. A label that calls the pattern a symbol of a whole community, with no source, is weak. People in one group may not all see an object in the same way. A better label uses evidence from the makers and users. It says what we know and what we still need to ask.
read.sections.2.text.back: Museum labels tell visitors about objects. The bag's first label only said "A bag for carrying everyday things", which is true, but it leaves out the memory and the skill. Guessing what the pattern means is not right either. A label that says the pattern is a symbol of the whole community, with no source to confirm it, is a weak label. People in the same group may not all see an object the same way. A better label uses evidence from makers and users, and says what we know and what we still need to ask.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: A museum label tells people about a thing. This label says “Everyday carrying bag”. That is true. But it misses the memory and the skill. Do not guess what the pattern means. Do not call it a symbol of a whole group. You need proof for that. A good label uses what the makers and users say. It also says what we still need to ask.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Museum labels tell people about objects. This label says "A bag for carrying everyday things", which is true, but it leaves out the memory and the skill. Don't guess what the pattern means. Don't call the pattern a symbol of the whole group. That needs evidence. A good label uses what makers and users say, and also says what we still need to ask.

watch.summary.note: Ayala Museum = พิพิธภัณฑ์อายาลา (transliteration; please confirm). salakot = ซาลาโกต, a Filipino hat.
watch.summary.source: This short video comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. It looks at three everyday objects from the museum. The first is a small green pot from China. Long ago, people in the Philippines traded for Chinese pots and bowls. Most were plain, but this one has two dragons on it. The second is the salakot, a wide hat woven from plants. Many ordinary people wore it. But some salakot were decorated with shell and silver for important people. The third is a small cloth called a handkerchief. If you look closely, you can see a sad poem sewn into it. The video says the materials and the skill make an object valuable. But the stories and context around it make it even more special.
watch.summary.back: This short video is from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. It looks at three everyday objects from the museum. The first is a small green pot from China. Long ago, people in the Philippines traded to get pots and bowls from China. Most were plain, but this one has two dragons on it. The second is a salakot, a wide-brimmed hat woven from plants. Many ordinary people wore this hat, but some salakots were decorated with shells and silver for important people. The third is a small cloth called a handkerchief. If you look closely you see a sad poem embroidered on the cloth. The video says materials and skill make objects valuable, but the stories and context around them make the objects even more special.
